newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia mulls oil export revamp to cut firms' debts.
newsitem.headline: Russia mulls oil export revamp to cut firms' debts.

text.p: Russia aims to reduce oil firms' tax debts by $2 billion by tightening a grip on their exports for state-sponsored projects and sending the money directly into the budget, the Fuel and Energy Ministry said Friday.

The move is not expected to affect the overall volume of oil exported from Russia. But it could mean exports which once funded state-sponsored projects and earned producers easy cash will now take place on a more commercial basis, which could affect producers' marketing strategies.
Under the new scheme, Moscow wants firms to pay a part of their oil export revenues directly into state coffers instead of into funds for the state-sponsored investment projects.
The plan envisages channelling eight percent of Russia's total oil export revenues directly into the budget.

"A share of the oil exports which went to funding state needs programmes would go towards paying off oil company debts (under the plan)," said Fuel and Energy Ministry spokesman Sergei Slesaryev. "The volumes exported will be the same."
Russia uses oil exports under so-called federal programmes to fund domestic projects ranging from satellite launches to Kremlin wall facelifts.

Oil industry sources said the scheme appeared to be aimed at cutting back on the Soviet-era system of funding state projects from oil export revenues -- a scheme which is bleeding Russia's nascent oil company sector of much-needed hard currency.
But Slesaryev said this was not the plan's principal aim.

"Once the debts are settled, the money will go into the budget, and it will then be decided where to distribute the money," he said, adding the plan would increase government control over the trade and export of raw materials.
"Government control of the flow of Russian goods is increasing (under the plan)," he said. "It is more realistic to control the flow of goods than it is the flow of finances."
State needs exports accounted for over a quarter of Russian oil exports by volume during the first three months of 1997.
The new scheme is consistent with Fuel and Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov's priority policy of pressuring the energy sector to pay off crippling debts.
Russia's key oil and gas sector owed a massive 28.85 trillion ($5.0 billion) to various budgets as of June 1.
First Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Sergei Kiriyenko told the weekly Itogi business magazine the government hoped the new scheme would raise $2 billion for the state by the end of 1997.
The plan was Moscow's best way to clamp down on debtors, Kiriyenko said, because the government still had control over the flow of oil along Russia's domestic and export pipeline system.
Russia exported 125.6 million tonnes (2.51 million barrels per day) of oil to all destinations in 1996.
